title: Tesla Profits Plunge as AI Spending Surges and EV Discounts Squeeze Margins
excerpt: Revenue beat expectations on record deliveries, but a 57% drop in operating income and Tesla's first cash burn in over two years rattled investors as Elon Musk doubles down on robotaxis and humanoid robots.
body:
• Tesla's adjusted earnings for Q2 were 33 cents per share, significantly below the expected 51 cents and down 18% from the previous year.
  • Despite record vehicle deliveries of 480,126, average revenue per vehicle dropped to $42,730 due to the introduction of lower-priced models.
  • Automotive gross margin fell to 16.3%, below analyst expectations, as the company faced increased costs from its AI initiatives and price cuts.
  • Regulatory credit revenue plummeted to $146 million, a significant decline from $439 million a year ago, due to changes in U.S. policy.

Tesla missed profit expectations by a wide margin in the second quarter even as it delivered a record number of vehicles, underscoring the steep cost of CEO Elon Musk's aggressive pivot toward artificial intelligence, robotaxis, and humanoid robots.

The Austin, Texas-based automaker reported adjusted earnings of 33 cents per share for the quarter ended June 30, well below the 51-cent consensus compiled by LSEG and 18% lower than the 40 cents it earned in Q2 2025. Revenue, however, climbed 26% year-over-year to $28.24 billion, comfortably ahead of the $25.7 billion analysts had forecast, according to Reuters.

Shares fell roughly 4.5% in extended trading on Wednesday, wiping about $58 billion from Tesla's $1.4 trillion market capitalisation.

Record Deliveries, Shrinking Margins

Tesla delivered 480,126 vehicles during the quarter, up 25% from a year ago and its strongest second-quarter performance on record. A war-induced fuel price surge drove EV demand in Europe, while incentives and stripped-down trims of the Model 3 and Model Y boosted sales in the United States, where the removal of the $7,500 federal EV tax credit last year had dampened demand.

But volume came at a price. Average revenue per vehicle fell to $42,730 from $45,345 a year earlier after Tesla discontinued its higher-end Model S sedan and Model X SUV and rolled out lower-priced trims. Automotive gross margin excluding regulatory credits slipped to 16.3%, down from 19% in Q1 and well below the 18% analysts had expected, according to Visible Alpha data.

"We already know it was a record delivery quarter, but if it was achieved through price cuts or other incentives, it will be read as a hollow beat."

— Bill Birmingham, Managing Director, REX Shares

Regulatory credit revenue — essentially pure profit for Tesla — cratered to $146 million from $439 million a year ago, as a U.S. policy change eroded the value of emissions credits sold to rival automakers.

The AI Spending Spree

The profit miss stems largely from Tesla's ballooning investment in what Musk calls "physical AI." Capital expenditures surged 142% to $5.79 billion in the quarter — more than double Q1's $2.5 billion — pushing free cash flow to negative $1.09 billion, the company's first cash burn since Q1 2024. Analysts had actually expected worse, projecting a $3.3 billion cash drain, according to FactSet.

Research and development spending climbed to $2.3 billion from $1.6 billion a year earlier, and total operating expenses rose 47% year-over-year to $4.35 billion. GAAP operating income fell 57% to $398 million, producing an operating margin of just 1.4%, down from 4.1% a year ago.

Tesla reiterated plans to spend roughly $25 billion on capital expenditures in 2026, nearly triple the $8.5 billion it spent in 2025. Musk defended the outlay on the post-earnings conference call.

"This is a massive capex year, but I'm confident that all the things that we are investing in will yield incredible returns."

— Elon Musk, CEO, Tesla

Robotaxi Caution, Optimus Delays

Investors waiting for concrete timelines on Tesla's next-generation products came away with little new information. Tesla's robotaxi service now operates in six cities — Austin, Dallas, Houston, Miami, Orlando, and Tampa — but Musk struck a cautious tone on expansion, warning that any accident would invite regulatory crackdowns. VP of AI Ashok Elluswamy cited an "impeccable record" of zero notable incidents across 380,000 miles of unsupervised driving and said future rollout would happen state by state rather than city by city.

On Optimus, Tesla's humanoid robot, Musk said production would begin "soon" — though the company had previously told investors to expect late July or August. Musk described Optimus as the hardest product Tesla has ever attempted to scale.

Full Self-Driving subscriptions offered a bright spot: Tesla reported 1.48 million FSD subscribers, up 56% year-over-year, with 55% of North American vehicle purchases including an FSD subscription at the time of sale, according to CFO Vaibhav Taneja.

What It Means for Indian-Origin Professionals and EV Watchers

Tesla's aggressive AI and robotics hiring spree has drawn heavily on Indian-origin engineering talent in Silicon Valley and Austin. CFO Taneja, himself Indian-American, has become one of the most prominent diaspora executives in the global auto industry. The company's pivot toward physical AI — and the $25 billion spending plan behind it — signals sustained demand for AI, semiconductor, and robotics expertise, a pipeline that Indian engineering graduates continue to feed.

For EV watchers in India, Tesla's margin compression on its core auto business illustrates the challenge any premium EV maker faces in a price-sensitive market. Tesla's average selling price of $42,730 still places its vehicles well above what most Indian consumers would consider, even as the company pushes toward affordability.

What's Next

Wall Street expects Tesla to deliver about 1.7 million vehicles in 2026. The company's services segment — including FSD subscriptions and Supercharger revenue — surged 50% to $4.6 billion and is emerging as a counterweight to auto margin pressure. Energy storage deployments hit a record 13.5 GWh in the quarter, up from 9.6 GWh a year earlier.

But the central question remains whether Musk's capital-intensive bets on autonomy and robotics will generate the returns needed to justify Tesla's premium valuation. With $43.5 billion in cash on hand and the option to borrow up to $30 billion in debt, Tesla has runway. Whether investors will stay patient through quarters of cash burn and margin compression is another matter.

"Monetization remains the central concern following the earnings miss," said Ryan Lee, senior vice president at Direxion. "The question is how quickly those investments can begin supporting the valuation."
